ATP7A is regulated in an opposite fashion in the intestine compared to peripheral tissues, and that the intestine-specific regulation of ATP 7A may be a key homeostasis control for Cu export.
ATP7A is inversely regulated in an organ-specific manner in response to Cu fluctuation.
ATP7A is differentially regulated in the intestine and peripheral tissues to coordinate Cu homeostasis and prevent Cu toxicity.

how the body controls the amount of copper in the blood.
understanding how the organism responds to changes in copper (Cu) homeostasis.
the mechanisms that regulate the abundance and activity of the Cu transporters ATP7A and ATP7B in the liver, heart, kidney, brain and other tissues in the body.

the regulation of intestinal ATP7A is inversely correlated to that of peripheral ATP7A, suggesting a non-autonomous mechanism for regulation of intestinal ATP 7A in response to systemic copper fluctuation.
the regulation of ATP7a in the liver and heart is coordinated with systemic Cu homeostasis and is inversely regulated in the small intestine.
ATP7A abundance in the intestine and peripheral tissues are inversely regulated in order to coordinate intestinal Cu export and systemic Cu homeostasis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the regulation of ATP7a abundance in peripheral tissues is inversely coordinated with the intestine to maintain systemic Cu homeostasis.
ATP7A abundance in peripheral tissues is inversely regulated with respect to systemic Cu status, while the intestine is inversely regulated.
intestinal ATP7A levels are inversely regulated with systemic Cu levels to maintain Cu export into the periphery.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single transporter can have different regulatory mechanisms depending on tissue and context.
the same transporter can be differentially regulated in distinct tissues, and this regulation is important for maintaining organismal Cu homeo-stasis.
ATP7A is regulated in a tissue-dependent manner to maintain Cu homeostasis and that this regulation occurs through a systemic mechanism.
